question: A budget owner compares two models. Model X has a lower price per token. Model Y finishes each task with fewer requests. The owner must choose on the cost of one completed task. Which measure meets the constraint?

choices.A: Sum the token prices across all requests for one completed task, then compare the totals.
choices.B: Compare the per-token list prices, since they are published and stable.
choices.C: Build a per-developer cost dashboard with attribution before any comparison.
choices.D: Read the price field in each Messages API response to compare the two models.

explanation: A lower token price does not show what a finished task costs. Compare models on cost per completed task, because you pay for completed tasks. Trap. The lower per-token price looks cheaper, but the model that needs more requests can cost more per completed task.

question: A proposal moves a quality-sensitive task to a cheaper model tier. The team has no test on its own tasks. The decision must rest on measured quality and cost for real traffic. Which step meets the constraint?

choices.A: Switch the task to the cheaper tier, since its per-token price is lower.
choices.B: Read the Usage and Cost API totals and treat them as a quality score for each answer.
choices.C: Sample production tasks weighted like real traffic, and plot each tier score against its spend.
choices.D: Rebuild the product on three providers, then run a six-month comparison on real traffic.

explanation: Production tasks show how each tier performs on real traffic. A score beside the spend shows whether the cheaper tier meets the bar at a lower cost per task. Trap. A switch on the lowest per-token price looks like a saving, but the team then has no evidence that the cheaper tier meets the bar.

question: A finance audience and a security audience review a model option. The vendor claims zero risk and perfect accuracy. The record must give each audience the facts it decides on. Select two entries that meet this constraint.

choices.A: Attach the Usage and Cost API export as proof of zero risk.
choices.B: State the cost per completed task with the date of the price list.
choices.C: Show the per-token list price alone as the cost field for each option.
choices.D: Name the measured accuracy with its evaluation set, and give an uncertainty beside it.

explanation: Finance decides on cost per completed task, and list prices drift over time. Security needs a measured figure with its evaluation set and uncertainty, not an absolute claim. (Inference) Trap. An attached usage export looks like evidence, but that report measures spend, not risk.

question: A finance lead wants daily cost totals in USD for each team workspace. The script must use credentials that the usage and cost endpoints accept. Which setup meets the constraint?

choices.A: Call the usage and cost endpoints with the workspace API key that the script already holds.
choices.B: Set the Cost API bucket to one minute to get finer daily totals.
choices.C: Stream each response usage field into a warehouse, and rebuild the totals every hour.
choices.D: Call the usage and cost endpoints with an Admin API key, and read the daily cost report by workspace.

explanation: The usage and cost endpoints accept Admin API credentials only, so a workspace key fails. The Cost report gives daily totals in USD, and it can group them by workspace. Trap. A workspace API key looks sufficient for a script, but the usage and cost endpoints do not accept workspace keys.

question: An on-call engineer must see a traffic spike within seconds. The team has a usage report and a cost report. The team cannot wait for a daily total. Which action meets the constraint?

choices.A: Poll the Usage and Cost API once per minute and alert on each new total.
choices.B: Set a monthly spend alert on the workspace to catch a spike within seconds.
choices.C: Read the usage fields in each live response, and log them as responses return.
choices.D: Add a live response log, and also run a weekly cost review with finance.

explanation: The aggregate reports typically lag each request by up to 5 minutes, so they are too slow for this check. Per-response usage fields report each call as it completes. Trap. Polling the usage endpoints every minute looks fast, but the aggregate data can trail each request by up to 5 minutes.

question: A company runs one workspace for each team. The owner wants a monthly budget for each team and rate limits for each model. Select two settings that meet both requests.

choices.A: Set a monthly spend limit and alerts on each team workspace.
choices.B: Set a per-minute spend limit on each workspace to cap traffic bursts.
choices.C: Set rate limits per model on requests, input tokens, and output tokens per minute.
choices.D: Put every team on the Default Workspace, and set one spend limit there.

explanation: A spend limit and its alerts apply to one workspace, so each team gets its own budget. Rate limits cap requests and tokens per minute for each model. Trap. One spend limit on the Default Workspace looks like a shared budget, but that workspace accepts no spend limit.

question: A decision record names a model by family only. A successor cannot tell which model the evaluation measured. The record must name the measured model exactly. Which entry meets the constraint?

choices.A: Attach the full evaluation notebook and every raw response to the record.
choices.B: Write the exact model ID and the platform in the record.
choices.C: Record the model family name only, since the family name identifies the model.
choices.D: Record the API version header as the model ID for the evaluation.

explanation: From the 4.6 generation on, a dateless ID names one fixed snapshot. The exact ID and the platform let a successor identify the measured model. Trap. A model family name looks like enough, but it does not name the snapshot that the evaluation measured.

question: A decision record names a model ID. The platform posts a retirement notice with a date for that ID. The notice names a replacement model. The team must keep the record accurate and avoid an outage on that date. Which action meets the constraint?

choices.A: Record the retirement date beside the ID, then test the named replacement before that date.
choices.B: Keep the ID in the record, since a dateless ID is a fixed snapshot that never retires.
choices.C: Freeze all model work for the year, and rebuild every decision record from scratch.
choices.D: Add the Usage page CSV to the record as the model version number.

explanation: Every model ID has its own retirement schedule, and a notice sets the date. A tested replacement lets the team move traffic before that date. Trap. A dateless ID looks permanent, but it is a fixed snapshot that still follows its own retirement schedule.

question: A team writes a decision record for a Claude model in production. A successor must run the system later and must check the decision. Select two entries that meet both needs.

choices.A: Record the model family and let the successor choose the newest model.
choices.B: Record the workspace spend limit as the model version for the decision.
choices.C: Record the exact model ID with its platform and deprecation date.
choices.D: Write the review criteria that reopen the decision as measurable thresholds.

explanation: The exact ID, the platform, and the deprecation date tell a successor what runs and when it retires. Measurable review criteria tell the successor when to reopen the decision. (Inference) Trap. A model family name looks like a stable reference, but it does not identify the snapshot that was measured.

question: A release moves the client to API version 2026-10-21. Every request now fails with a 400 error, because the client sends a temperature value. The fix must remove the cause and pass a test gate before release. Which action meets the constraint?

choices.A: Keep the temperature value, and add a retry with backoff, since the error may clear.
choices.B: Raise the workspace rate limit, so that the 400 errors clear.
choices.C: Remove the temperature value, and also rewrite the prompts and logs before the test gate.
choices.D: Remove the temperature value from each request, then run the test gate before release.

explanation: The 400 error comes from a parameter that the new API version removes. The parameter removal fixes the cause, and the test gate confirms the release before traffic moves. (Inference) Trap. A retry with backoff looks like a standard fix, but the parameter itself causes the 400 error on each request.

question: A deprecation notice names a retirement date for a model that the production service calls. The notice names a replacement. The team must avoid an outage on the retirement date. Which action meets the constraint?

choices.A: Wait for the retirement date, then switch the model in one release.
choices.B: Export usage by API key and model, test the named replacement, and move traffic before the date.
choices.C: Move the whole product to a new cloud platform, and rewrite its prompts before the date.
choices.D: Keep the retired model on a backup route, which still returns answers after the date.

explanation: The usage export lists each API key and model, so the team finds every caller of the old model. The test and the move come before the date, because requests to a retired model fail. Trap. A switch at the retirement date looks simple, but requests to a retired model fail after that date.

question: A team runs development and production traffic in one shared workspace. The team needs separate rate limits and separate cost reports for each environment. Select two changes that meet both requests.

choices.A: Create a production workspace, and scope the production API key to it.
choices.B: Rename the Default Workspace to production, since the Default Workspace can be renamed.
choices.C: Create a development workspace, and set lower rate limits on it than on production.
choices.D: Keep one workspace, and add an environment label to each API key name.

explanation: Each request runs in exactly one workspace, so each environment needs its own workspace for keys, limits, and reports. The Default Workspace cannot be renamed, so the team creates new workspaces instead. Trap. A rename of the Default Workspace looks like the quickest split, but that workspace cannot be renamed.

question: A team wants the agent to never read files in a secrets folder, in every clone. A note in CLAUDE.md asks the agent to avoid that folder. The block must hold even when the model ignores the note. Which change meets the constraint?

choices.A: Deploy the deny rule in managed settings, and add a sandbox on every developer machine.
choices.B: Add the deny rule to the personal local settings of the team lead only.
choices.C: Add a Read deny rule for the secrets folder in the committed settings file.
choices.D: Add a PostToolUse hook that blocks reads of the secrets folder.

explanation: A deny rule in the committed settings file reaches every clone after a pull. The rule blocks the read before the tool runs, so the result does not depend on the model. Trap. A PostToolUse hook that blocks reads looks like enforcement, but that hook runs only after the tool call succeeds.

question: A team wants a research subagent that only reads files. The subagent must not receive any write tool. Which setup meets the constraint?

choices.A: Set the tools field to Read and Grep, and add a second reviewer subagent for each folder.
choices.B: Create the subagent without a tools field, and add a CLAUDE.md line that forbids edits.
choices.C: Set the model field to read-only, which blocks write tools for the subagent.
choices.D: Set the subagent tools field to Read and Grep only.

explanation: The tools field limits the tools that a subagent can use. Read and Grep cannot write files, so the role stays read-only. Trap. A CLAUDE.md line that forbids edits looks like a restriction, but a subagent without a tools field inherits every tool.

question: A team needs one enforced rule on every clone. One developer also needs a personal exception that does not weaken the team rule. Select two actions that meet both needs.

choices.A: Commit the team deny rule in the shared settings file.
choices.B: Put the team deny rule in the user settings file of each developer.
choices.C: Put a personal allow rule for one extra command in the local settings file, which stays out of git.
choices.D: Put the team deny rule in CLAUDE.md, which Claude Code enforces as a permission.

explanation: The shared settings file applies to every clone after a pull. The local file stays out of git, and a deny rule from any scope still applies. Trap. A personal settings file looks flexible, but it cannot enforce the rule across the team.

question: A CI job runs Claude Code to check a pull request. The job must restrict the run to the Read and Grep tools. A failed run must fail the job. Which command setup meets both constraints?

choices.A: Run claude -p with --allowedTools set to Read and Grep, then check the exit status.
choices.B: Run claude -p with --json-schema, which limits the tools that the run can use.
choices.C: Run claude -p with --tools set to Read and Grep, then check the exit status in the next CI step.
choices.D: Run claude -p with --tools set to Read and Grep, check the exit status, and store every transcript in a database.

explanation: The --tools flag restricts which built-in tools exist for the run. The exit status tells the CI step whether the run succeeded. Trap. An --allowedTools list looks like a restriction, but the flag only lets the listed tools run without a prompt.

question: A script runs Claude Code and reads one typed field from the reply. The script must also record the total cost of each run. Which setup meets both constraints?

choices.A: Run with --output-format json and --json-schema, then read structured_output and total_cost_usd.
choices.B: Parse the free-text reply with a pattern match, and skip the cost field.
choices.C: Run with --output-format json and --json-schema, and store every full transcript in a database.
choices.D: Run with --tools set to a fixed list, and read the per-model breakdown from the --tools output.

explanation: The json output format with a schema returns typed fields in structured_output. The JSON output also includes total_cost_usd for each run. Trap. A pattern match on free text looks simple, but it gives the script no typed field and no cost value.

question: A team wants one credential for six repositories that run comment-triggered workflows. The credential must not depend on the subscription of one person. Select two actions that meet the constraint.

choices.A: Run the setup-token command, and store the OAuth token as one organization-level secret.
choices.B: Create an API key in the Claude Console for the shared secret.
choices.C: Set the use_bedrock input to true, which shares one credential across repositories.
choices.D: Store one organization-level Actions secret that all six repositories share.

explanation: The OAuth token is tied to one subscription, but an API key from the Claude Console can serve a shared secret. An organization-level Actions secret lets the repositories share one stored copy. Trap. An OAuth token from the setup command looks easy to share, but it is tied to the subscription of one person.

question: A hook in the shared settings file does not run after edits. The team must find out whether the hook is loaded. The check must not change any file. Which action meets the constraint?

choices.A: Run /hooks, then start with claude --debug, and export the metrics to a collector.
choices.B: Run /hooks in the current session to see the hook configuration.
choices.C: Add a CLAUDE.md line that asks Claude to run the hook after each edit.
choices.D: Run /context to list each hook match and its exit code.

explanation: The /hooks command shows the hook configurations in the current session. The command only reads configuration, so no file changes. Trap. A CLAUDE.md line that asks for the hook looks like a fix, but a guidance note never starts a hook.

question: Cost rose after a prompt change in the sessions of one team. The team must find the cause before it changes the model. The first step must use per-session data. Which action meets the constraint?

choices.A: Switch to a smaller model at once, since a smaller model lowers the cost of each session.
choices.B: Check claude_code.session.count to see the cost of each prompt.
choices.C: Run /usage in each affected session to read its cost.
choices.D: Export OpenTelemetry metrics to a team collector, and build a cost dashboard before any session is checked.

explanation: The /usage command shows the cost of the current session. Per-session cost identifies the affected sessions before any model change. Trap. A smaller model looks like the fastest cost fix, but it may miss the cause and can lower answer quality.

question: An agent edit must be undone. Some changes came from a Bash command that changed files Claude never edited. The undo must cover both kinds of change. Select two actions that meet the constraint.

choices.A: Use /rewind to undo the tracked Claude edits from the recent checkpoints.
choices.B: Press Esc twice to rewind the Bash-only file change, since rewind covers every change.
choices.C: Set cleanupPeriodDays to 90 to restore snapshots that were already deleted.
choices.D: Use version control to revert the files that only the Bash command changed.

explanation: Rewind restores file edits that Claude tracked, within the checkpoints that the session keeps. Files that only a Bash command changed are not tracked, so version control reverts them. Trap. A double Esc press looks like a full undo, but rewind does not track Bash changes to files that Claude never edited.
